name: Propolis

lead: Propolis is the resin bees blend with wax to seal their hives. A K-beauty staple in ampoules and creams, it is used to calm breakouts, soothe skin and give a glowy finish, building on a long folk-medicine history.

Lab studies attribute antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity to its flavonoids and phenolics, including CAPE, which inhibits NF-kappa B signalling in cell experiments. Composition varies widely by origin. Human trials on cosmetic skin outcomes were not found; registered clinical trials concern uses such as oral health.

paras: People use propolis ampoules, creams and spot treatments as part of layered K-beauty routines, often for blemish-prone, irritated or dull skin. It is also sold as a supplement.

Contact allergy is the main documented risk, with skin inflammation and lip swelling reported from topical products, especially in people sensitive to bee products. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient and supplement; no special approval for skin benefits is reported.

angle.text: Propolis is used in K-beauty ampoules and creams to calm breakouts, soothe skin and give a glowy finish. Lab studies show antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity; skin-specific human trials were not found.

lead: Propolis, also called bee glue, is a sticky resinous mixture that honey bees make from plant exudates such as tree-bud resins and sap, combined with beeswax and saliva. Bees use it to seal gaps in the hive and to coat its interior surfaces [1][2]. Its composition varies with the hive's location, season and local plants, and it typically includes flavonoids, phenolic acids and terpenoids [2].

In skincare, propolis appears as an extract in K-beauty and natural-cosmetic products, where brands market it for soothing, blemish-prone and dull-looking skin. The route to a better-looking complexion that proponents describe runs through calming irritation, supporting a clearer-looking surface and giving a glow, drawing on propolis's long traditional use and on laboratory findings of antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity [3][4][5].

A 2020 review of bee products in dermatology and skin care describes propolis, honey, pollen, royal jelly and beeswax as possible ingredients for skin-applied medicines and cosmetics [5]. Most of the propolis literature consists of laboratory and review work on its constituents, and clinical trials registered for propolis concern other uses such as oral health, wound care and general medicine [6][7][8][9]. Propolis is also a recognised cause of allergic contact dermatitis [2][10].

paras: Honey bees make propolis by combining plant exudates, such as resin from tree buds and sap flows, with saliva and beeswax. They use it to fill small gaps in the hive, strengthen the structure, insulate it and narrow the entrance, and they line the nest with it. Wikipedia links this lining to the colony's 'social immunity', its collective defence against pathogens, and notes that bees can seal dead intruders they cannot remove inside propolis [2].

Propolis is usually dark brown but can also be green, red, black or white. It is sticky above about 19 C and hard and brittle at lower temperatures [2]. Stingless bees and Apis mellifera honeybees both produce it, and it occurs in tropical and subtropical forests worldwide [9].

Propolis is a variable natural product. Its chemistry depends on the plants bees visit, and researchers classify it by botanical source into poplar-type in temperate regions, birch-type, Mediterranean and Pacific types and tropical varieties such as Brazilian green propolis (from Baccharis dracunculifolia), which is rich in artepillin C, and Brazilian red propolis (from Dalbergia ecastaphyllum) [1][2]. Hundreds of constituents have been identified, including flavonoids, phenolic acids and terpenoids [2]. Fixed percentage breakdowns of resin, wax, oils and pollen are often quoted, but Wikipedia notes these are not well substantiated [2].

Flavonoids are a major constituent class and have been reviewed for antimicrobial and other biological activities [11][12]. Reviews of propolis name compounds such as artepillin C, caffeic acid, CAPE, apigenin, chrysin, galangin and kaempferol among its biologically active constituents [9]. Caffeic acid phenethyl ester (CAPE) inhibited activation of the transcription factor NF-kappa B in a 1996 laboratory study [13]. The variability between samples makes standardisation difficult and complicates comparison across studies [12][14][2].

Propolis extracts are included in serums, ampoules, masks and spot treatments sold in Korean and natural-skincare lines, usually with claims about calming, hydrating or clarifying skin. The 2020 review of bee products in dermatology says that honey, propolis and pollen are used to heal burn wounds and have been described as antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, disinfectant, antifungal and antiviral, and that bee products could be important ingredients in skin-applied medicines and cosmetics [5]. A 2023 narrative review of alternative treatments for herpes simplex lists propolis among natural products that showed promise in controlling the virus, relevant to cold sores on the lips [15]. No cosmetic-specific trial listed in the reviews quantifies effects on wrinkles, pigmentation or acne [5][9].

Writers describe propolis use in traditional medicine since antiquity, including wound care and antiseptic applications in Egyptian, Greek and Roman sources, though dating claims come from secondary summaries [1]. Researchers have reviewed its antibacterial, antifungal and antiviral activity across propolis of different geographic origin [4], a 2019 review analysed its effect on more than 600 bacterial strains, finding greater activity against Gram-positive than Gram-negative bacteria and highest activity in Middle Eastern samples [16], and its potential as a source of new drugs has been discussed [12]. Propolis is also sold as a supplement, and it has been used in oral-care products [2][7].
Some string-instrument makers use propolis as a varnish ingredient or to seal new violin-family bridges. Wikipedia notes that claims that Antonio Stradivari used it were disproven in 2009 [2].

Laboratory research attributes propolis's activity to its flavonoids and phenolic compounds. CAPE blocks NF-kappa B activation in cell experiments, a pathway central to inflammatory signalling [13]. Flavonoids have been reviewed for antimicrobial effects [11], and propolis extracts act against a range of bacteria, fungi and viruses in vitro [4][16]. Reviews of propolis as complementary medicine link its constituents to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory and other activities [9]. These findings come from laboratory and animal studies and from reviews of them; they are not direct measures of cosmetic skin outcomes [12][14].

Clinical research on propolis as a whole is mostly outside skincare. Registered or completed trials have examined propolis for hand-foot-and-mouth disease, COVID-19, mouthwash and periodontal health, radiotherapy-induced oral mucositis, dentin hypersensitivity, insulin resistance and cardiometabolic outcomes [6][7][8]. Randomised trials include a comparison of propolis with a desensitising agent for dentin hypersensitivity [17], a double-blind trial of propolis versus metformin versus placebo in 36 treatment-naive patients with type 2 diabetes [18], a trial of propolis in people with metabolic syndrome examining mood, quality of life and metabolic profile [19], a trial of standardised Brazilian green propolis extract in COVID-19 [20][21], and a 2024 trial of Brazilian green propolis for chronic ulcers [22].

Wikipedia reports that a 2026 review of 45 trials found possible reductions in dental plaque and oral microbes with very low certainty, that mucositis studies were small with blinding problems, and that a meta-analysis of 20 trials found lower fasting glucose and triglycerides without significant changes in blood pressure, waist circumference or HDL cholesterol [2]. A review of anticancer activity covers laboratory work on propolis and its compounds [23].
No controlled human study of topical propolis for wrinkles, skin tone or acne has been published.

Propolis can cause allergic contact dermatitis, with reported reactions to topical products including skin inflammation, lip swelling and cheilitis [2]. A 1983 study by Rudzki and Grzywa in Contact Dermatitis examined 22 patients with propolis dermatitis; all 21 tested reacted to propolis, and 19 also reacted to balsam of Peru, whose chromatograms resembled propolis's, with shared components such as cinnamyl cinnamate and vanillin implicated in some patients [10]. A 1998 review of its biological properties and toxicity addressed both benefits and adverse effects [3].

In appearance culture propolis appears mainly in K-beauty and natural-cosmetic lines, where it is marketed alongside honey and royal jelly for glow and calming claims [5]. It is also taken as a supplement alongside other bee products such as royal jelly and bee pollen. Brazilian green propolis extracts in particular have been developed as standardised products and studied in clinical trials, including in hospitalised COVID-19 patients [20][21].
Propolis is sold as a cosmetic ingredient and as a dietary supplement; its use for medical conditions is being tested in registered clinical trials [6][7][8].

Laboratory research continues on propolis flavonoids and phenolics, including anti-inflammatory signalling and antimicrobial activity [13][11][14]. Reviews describe the variability between propolis samples as a challenge for standardisation and for comparing studies [12][14]. Studies in other fields continue in registered trials of dental, metabolic and cardiovascular outcomes [6][7][8].

lore.intro: Propolis appears in skincare marketing and among bee-product supplements; community discussion of it for appearance is limited, and most commentary comes from K-beauty and natural-cosmetics brands. [5]
